column4: The livestock carry human loads to a land reachable only with severe strain; this is the section's laden journey-animal, while the closing mercy identifies the mount itself as divine relief.
Pilgrims arrive “on every lean camel” from every distant pass; the animal's leanness after a long road directly realizes the source-section sense of a camel worn thin by journeys.
God makes ships and livestock into things people ride; this supplies the actual mounts whose backs, remembrance, and homeward orientation are developed in 43:13-14.
Settling on the mounts' ظُهُورِهِ and remembering the Lord's blessing joins the section's mount-back, rider, divine gift, and zikr in one act.
The mounted travel prayer ends “to our Lord we are returning,” exactly joining a ride to the section's road whose destination is Rabb.
The lost carry their أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ; the same burden-and-back configuration turns people into the load-bearing animals of their own wrongdoing.
The brothers ask for an added كَيْلَ بَعِيرٍ and call it كَيْلٌ يَسِيرٌ; a camel-load and ease meet explicitly inside a provisioned caravan.
The oath by “those bearing a load,” فَالْحَامِلَاتِ وِقْرًا, isolates the section's first caravan feature: a bearer defined by what rests upon it.
The next oath, فَالْجَارِيَاتِ يُسْرًا, makes easy motion follow load-bearing, the same sequence as the laden animal whose gait becomes tractable.
Road thirst and نَصَب are credited as righteous work, while وَلَا يَرْغَبُوا links that fatigue to directed preference; both of the section's final roots operate in one journey.
Moses refuses to cease travelling until he reaches the meeting of the seas; sustained road effort is ordered by a fixed destination.
After passing the meeting place, Moses names what the section stages: لَقِينَا مِن سَفَرِنَا هَٰذَا نَصَبًا, fatigue encountered through travel.
The “abode of lasting residence” is the reached station where لَا يَمَسُّنَا فِيهَا نَصَبٌ; destination, permanent stay, and the ending of road-fatigue coincide.
Paradise contains no نَصَب and its people are never expelled; it precisely combines release from journey-weariness with the section's final place that is never left.
The command to look at the camel makes the section's load-bearing mount itself an object of reflective attention.
Immediately above the camel scene, the sky is رُفِعَتْ; the section hears this same root as the mount's raised pace.
The mountains are نُصِبَتْ in the next view; this turns the section's root for sustained travel and fatigue into the firmly erected landmarks of its landscape.
The Messenger يَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ, removing people's burden from them; its syntax and relief closely match the section's load being put down from the addressed traveler.
The prayer asks the Lord not to place a crushing obligation upon the speakers or load them beyond capacity; it voices the human side of the burden the section says was removed.
سَيَجْعَلُ اللَّهُ بَعْدَ عُسْرٍ يُسْرًا states the hard-to-easy passage as a divinely made succession, matching the section's resistant and tractable mounts.
God wills اليُسْر and does not will العُسْر; the legal context states as divine intention the opposition that the section embodies as two kinds of mount.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَى portrays the rightly oriented person as being made ready for ease, like the section's responsive animal made fit to proceed.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْعُسْرَى deliberately couples facilitation with the hard end; it exposes that the road one is made ready for can itself be difficulty.
God tells the same prophetic addressee وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَى; divine preparation makes the traveler fit for the easy course rather than merely promising ease around him.
The human being labors “toward your Lord” and will meet Him; exertion, direction, and arrival reproduce the section's whole road in one address.
إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ الْمُسْتَقَرُّ names the Lord as the final settled place, closely matching the caravan's destination where it remains.
No bearer carries another's burden, and the verse ends with return to “your Lord”; distribution of loads and the journey's divine endpoint appear together.
The repeated rule that no bearer bears another's load is followed by “to your Lord is your return,” again joining burden-accounting to arrival at Rabb.
A heavily laden soul may call for help, yet none of its load is carried; this sets the limit of the section's mercy-image of a creature carrying another's weight.
Misleaders carry their own burdens and some burdens of those they misled; moral influence becomes an added load rather than the removed burden of the section.
They will carry their loads and further loads with them; the repeated حمل image turns wrongdoing into an accumulating caravan burden.
Whoever turns away from the reminder will carry a وِزْر on Resurrection Day; the section's physical load makes this otherwise moral burden perceptible.
The bearer remains under that burden and it is an evil load on Resurrection Day; this verse supplies the enduring pressure of the وِزْر introduced in 20:100.
God creates from livestock حَمُولَةً, animals of burden; this is the Qur'anic category to which the section's load-bearing caravan beast belongs.
Livestock have beauty when brought home and when sent out to pasture; the two daily movements supply the section's stopping and grazing life around the road.
Horses, mules, and donkeys are created لِتَرْكَبُوهَا; it extends the load-bearing mercy of 16:7 into the explicit act of riding.
People are carried on livestock and ships; the verse states transport as the shared gift behind the section's mount and the paired vehicles of 43:12.
God makes livestock tractable, ذَلَّلْنَاهَا لَهُمْ, so some become their rides; this directly corresponds to the section's compliant, easily guided mount.
God makes livestock so that people may ride some and eat from others; the riding animal is explicitly a divine provision.
Livestock meet needs carried in human breasts, and people are carried on them and on ships; need, load, and conveyance complete 40:79's gift.
Human beings are carried on land and sea and supplied with good things; carriage and road provision are presented together as honor.
Those who ask the Prophet for mounts weep when none can be found to carry them; the absent ride reveals how decisive the section's load-bearing gift is for a journey.
وَلَأَوْضَعُوا خِلَالَكُمْ uses the section's gait-root for harmful rushing among the believers; the easy-paced dictionary branch is sharply redirected into disruptive speed.
A caravan halts and sends its water-drawer, who lowers his bucket; it joins caravan movement to the water-stop developed in the section.
The travelers' merchandise is put into their رِحَال, the very saddle-baggage named in the source section's creaking-load definition.
Joseph places the drinking cup in his brother's رَحْل after loading the travelers; saddle-baggage and water equipment meet in one caravan act.
The reward is حِمْلُ بَعِيرٍ, a camel-load of grain; the mount's carrying capacity becomes the unit of promised provision.
The winter and summer caravan journeys make recurrent travel itself the community's ordered livelihood.
After naming the two journeys, the passage commands worship of the Lord of the House; the caravan road is given its Rabb and destination.
That Lord feeds against hunger and secures against fear; the journey's provision and safety explain why its destination is remembered as gift.
The she-camel has a fixed drinking turn and the people theirs on a known day; this is the section's daily watering-place rendered as an apportioned schedule.
The water is divided between the people and the she-camel, each turn attended; it directly stages regulated arrival at water.
The messenger says “Allah's she-camel and her drink”; animal, divine ownership, and the protected water-share are compressed into one warning.
Moses reaches Midian's water and finds a community watering their herds while two women hold theirs back; it is a full pastoral water-stop scene.
Moses waters the women's animals and then withdraws to shade; watering followed by departure closely parallels the section's camels leaving the water.
Allah's she-camel is left to graze on God's earth; it directly supplies the section's camel remaining in pasture and frames that access as a sign.
The same she-camel is to feed freely in God's earth and remain unharmed; the pasture is a protected provision rather than mere scenery.
God sends water from which people drink and vegetation in which they pasture animals; watering and grazing are joined as road-side provision.
People eat and pasture their livestock in the vegetation brought out along the earth's roads; human and mount are provisioned together.
The servants of the Merciful walk upon the earth هَوْنًا, gently; this human gait is the moral analogue of the section's calm, easy-going mount.
“Be measured in your walk and lower your voice” joins moderated pace to controlled sound, matching both the easy gait and the travel sounds developed in the section.
God رَفَعَ the sky and وَضَعَ the balance; the section's low and raised paces appear here as a deliberately paired cosmic ordering.
The Event is خَافِضَةٌ رَّافِعَةٌ, lowering and raising; this compact reversal illuminates the two opposed levels heard in the animal's gait.
The woman who unravels her yarn after it was strong gives نَقْض its physical dismantling force; it clarifies the source-section claim that long journeys seem to unravel the camel.
The wall يُرِيدُ أَن يَنقَضَّ, is about to collapse; this physical giving-way is the closest Qur'anic parallel to the worn mount seemingly broken apart by travel.
حَتَّىٰ تَضَعَ الْحَرْبُ أَوْزَارَهَا makes war lay down its burdens; the section's paired “put down” and “load” reappears as the ending of conflict.
Job names نُصْبٍ وَعَذَابٍ as the affliction that touched him; the root heard as all-day travel here retains its bodily weariness.
The scrolls' rule that no laden soul bears another's burden supplies another direct boundary for who can carry the section's load.
The believers did not spur either horses or رِكَاب against these settlements; the very riding-stock named by the source definition appears in a journey explicitly not made.
Many creatures do not carry their own provision, yet God sustains them and humans; this reverses the load-bearing beast and separates carrying from being provided for.
The donkey carrying books bears a real load without receiving their guidance; it exposes the boundary between transporting weight and inwardly carrying meaning.
The prized pregnant she-camels are abandoned at the Hour; the ordered, useful caravan dissolves so completely that even its most valued animals are left.
The camel cannot pass through a needle's eye; the broad load-bearing traveler meets an aperture that no gait or tractability can overcome.
The condemned drink boiling water like desperately thirsty camels; the familiar watering-stop becomes insatiable and punitive rather than merciful provision.
Pharaoh leads his people into the Fire and it is called an evil watering-place; a leader's herd-like arrival at water becomes the opposite of safe guidance and refreshment.
The people hamstring the she-camel after her protected pasture is announced; they destroy the very animal entrusted to them as a sign and provision.
After the command to let the she-camel graze, they hamstring her and receive a final three-day respite; settled pasture turns into irreversible departure.
They are warned not to harm the she-camel after her drinking share is fixed; the verse marks the boundary around the watering gift.
They hamstring her and then regret it; the water-sharing order of 26:155 is destroyed by the people it sustained.
The she-camel is sent as a trial, and the prophet must watch and be patient; the mount-like animal is here a test whose treatment measures the people.
They call their companion and hamstring the she-camel; this is the violent undoing of the apportioned watering scene in 54:28.
They deny the messenger and hamstring Allah's she-camel; rejection destroys both the animal and the protected drink named in 91:13.
The panting chargers stage the elevated, exhausting pace opposite the section's easy and gentle animal gait.
The chargers strike sparks, giving the fast gait a hoof-beat intensity absent from the calm caravan pace.
Their dawn charge turns animal movement from measured travel into attack.
The charge raises a cloud of dust; the road itself registers the violence of the faster tempo.
The riders penetrate the center of a host; this supplies the destination of the rapid mounted sequence, a hostile gathering rather than rest with Rabb.
The prohibition on swaggering over the earth supplies the proud gait against which 31:19's measured walk, and the section's easy pace, are heard.
The arrogant walker can neither split the earth nor reach the mountains in height; human pretension cannot turn an elevated gait into true elevation.
The trumpet ushers in يَوْمٌ عَسِيرٌ; hardship here is the destination-day itself rather than a difficult mount that can become easy.
That hard day is عَلَى الْكَافِرِينَ غَيْرُ يَسِيرٍ; explicit denial of ease fixes the far boundary of the section's promised tractability.
Joseph fully provisions the travelers and then conditions their next return; caravan equipment and the future road are planned together.
The brothers appeal to the caravan in which they returned as a witness; the عِير is a travelling community, not only a set of animals.
When the caravan departs, Jacob senses Joseph's scent; the moment of setting out makes the caravan carry news before its riders arrive.
At the confluence the travelers forget the fish and it takes its path into the sea; this is the missed arrival whose consequences produce the fatigue named in 18:62.
The servant recalls their rest at the rock and the fish's extraordinary path; a stopping-place, forgotten provision, and route-recognition meet here.
Moses identifies the sought place and the pair retrace their footprints; reaching the true destination requires turning back along the road already travelled.
The subdued livestock provide further benefits and drinks; riding in 36:72 is thus surrounded by the same provision and watering that sustain the section's road.
God makes the earth a cradle and puts roads in it so people may be guided; it lays out the traversable ground immediately before 43:12-14's mounts and travel prayer.
God spreads the earth and threads it with roads before bringing out pasture; route and grazing-ground form the terrain completed in 20:54.
God places landmarks and roads so people may be guided; these are the divinely fitted ways on which the section's caravan can travel.
Broad passes are made through the mountains as roads so people may be guided; it gives the caravan a traversable opening through raised terrain.
The earth is made an expanse for people, preparing the broad movement named in the next verse.
People travel through its فِجَاجًا سُبُلًا, broad passes as roads; this corresponds to the section's wide-stepping animal and ample way.
The earth is spread out beneath the camel, raised sky, and erected mountains; it completes the road-landscape of 88:17-19.
A near gain and moderate journey would have drawn the hypocrites, but the distance seemed hard; willingness is exposed by how demanding the road appears.
Humanity is created in toil, كَبَد; it gives the section's road-weariness a general human analogue without specifying travel.
The heavens, earth, and mountains refuse the Trust, but the human being carries it; an immense nonphysical charge is made intelligible as a borne load.
The rule that no burdened soul bears another's burden repeats the moral limit implicit in the section's individualized load.
God wishes to lighten the human burden because humanity was created weak; it states the mercy that the section renders as weight removed from a strained back.
God now lightens the believers' demand after acknowledging weakness among them; capacity determines how much weight is laid upon the traveler.
God does not intend to place constriction upon believers; this gives the hard/easy mount image a legal and purifying counterpart.
God places no constriction in the religion and names Abraham as forefather; the road toward Him is fitted rather than made impassable.
Whoever is mindful of God is granted يُسْرًا in his affair; ease is made as a consequence of right orientation.
Moses asks his Lord to make his task easy; prophetic work is imagined as something whose difficulty can be rendered tractable.
God says the Quran has been made easy for remembrance; the source-section quality of an easily guided, quickly responsive mount becomes an analogy for accessible instruction.
The repeated declaration that the Quran is made easy reinforces ease as an enacted divine making, not merely a favorable circumstance.
The third refrain again presents remembered revelation as something God renders tractable, echoing the section's compliant conveyance.
The final repetition keeps ease tied to remembrance, linking the section's easy movement back to the rider's zikr in 43:13.
The prophets call upon God رَغَبًا وَرَهَبًا, in longing and fear; رغبة here is directed devotional orientation rather than the source dictionary's wide stride.
مَن يَرْغَبُ عَن مِّلَّةِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ uses رغبة with “away from”; it clarifies by reversal the directional force of desiring toward the Lord.
Abraham's father asks whether he is turning away, أَرَاغِبٌ أَنتَ عَنْ آلِهَتِي; this false-godward threat sharpens the section's opposite orientation toward Rabb.
يَصْدُرُ النَّاسُ أَشْتَاتًا pictures people issuing forth in separate groups; the source dictionary sense “camels depart the water” supplies a concrete herd-motion behind the verb.
People emerge rapidly as though rushing toward a نُصُب; the section's root for sustained travel becomes an erected goal approached at an ominous pace.
The ark's course and anchorage are both in God's name; an alternate vehicle has its movement and settled endpoint held by Rabb, like the section's caravan.
The prophetic addressee has “a long movement/occupation” by day; it corresponds to the section's all-day exertion before renewed devotion.
Quraysh's cultivated familiarity anchors the two seasonal caravan journeys of 106:2 as an established communal rhythm.

The verse's الظَّهِيرَة fixes the noon-time sense embedded in the source dictionary's ظاهرة, “camels coming to water daily at noon”; the Qur'anic context itself concerns household privacy rather than watering.
Human offspring are carried in the laden ship, الْفُلْكِ الْمَشْحُونِ; this transfers the section's load-bearing vehicle from camel-back to a vessel filled for travel.
God creates for people counterparts to the laden ship that they ride; the neighbouring verses explicitly connect a loaded vehicle with other rideable conveyances.
The sacrificial camels stand in ordered rows while God's name is pronounced, then fall upon their sides and feed others; posture, animal provision, remembrance, and lowering all meet in one scene.
The animals are subjected to people so they may magnify God for His guidance and give thanks; tractability again leads the rider or handler to remembrance of the Giver.
God carries people over land and sea, but favorable travel turns into a storm in which they call on Him sincerely; the journey-prayer arises under threat rather than after calmly mounting.
The Lord drives ships through the sea so travelers can seek His bounty, and the verse names His mercy toward them; conveyance, provision, and Rabb's care coincide.
God subjects what is on earth and makes ships run by His command, closing with divine compassion and mercy; the moving vehicle is fitted and sustained as a gift.
After settling on the ark, the rider is commanded to praise God for deliverance; arriving and becoming established upon a vehicle elicit the remembrance voiced in 43:13.
The prayer asks “My Lord, cause me to land at a blessed landing”; Rabb is invoked as the one who grants the journey its good stopping-place.

A mother carries her child through weakness upon weakness, gratitude is commanded, and the destination is “to Me”; borne weight, exhaustion, thanks, and divine arrival form the section's sequence in human terms.
The mother حَمَلَتْهُ كُرْهًا وَوَضَعَتْهُ كُرْهًا, carrying and laying down in hardship; the section's load and its removal are joined in one bodily ordeal.
The blessed towns have visible, measured stages between them, and travelers are told to journey by night and day in safety; this is a divinely fitted caravan road with successive stopping-places.
The people ask for their journey-stages to be lengthened, then are scattered; rejection turns the measured, safe route of 34:18 into distance and dispersal.
Every valley the travelers cross is credited to them as a righteous deed; it continues 9:120 by making the actual ground covered part of the rewarded fatigue.
“To your Lord is the final limit” gives the section's caravan-road its ultimate terminus in the same direct second-person address.
The reassured soul is told to return to its Lord, pleased and pleasing; arrival at Rabb is an invited homecoming.
Fine, swift horses are presented to Solomon in the evening; this directly supplies the section's horse, rider, and elevated pace.
Solomon's attention to the good horses is explicitly related to remembrance of his Lord; the mounted animal and zikr meet, though the precise force of his statement is debated.

Fine horses and livestock are objects of worldly desire, while the verse ends by locating the good return with God; attachment to the mount is set against desire directed toward the final destination.
God brings the earth's water and pasture out of it; these are the two provisions at which the section's travelling animal drinks and remains.
Water, pasture, and fixed mountains are declared provision for people and their livestock; traveler and mount receive the road's resources together.
At Badr the believers occupy one side of the valley, the enemy the other, and the caravan is lower down; a moving caravan is located precisely within the road-landscape.
When people board a ship they call upon God sincerely, but after rescue to land they associate partners; the mounted remembrance of 43:13-14 is abandoned at journey's end.
Hell's thrown sparks are likened to tawny camels; the familiar road animal becomes the scale and shape of a terrifying projectile rather than a merciful conveyance.
At the Hour every pregnant creature lays down its حمل; putting down a carried load here marks cosmic terror rather than relief granted along the road.
Satan is told to incite with his voice and rally his cavalry and infantry; voice and mounted force form a dark reversal of the rider's guiding sound and Godward travel.
Noah and his companions are saved in a laden ship; a heavily loaded conveyance becomes the means by which its passengers reach safety.
Jonah flees to the laden ship; the same full vehicle that can signify rescue here begins a journey undertaken in flight.
Ships run through the sea carrying what benefits people; burden-bearing transport is placed among the signs of providentially ordered creation.
God subjects ships to run by His command and subjects the rivers; the journey's vehicle and waterway are both made tractable.
God sends winds so ships may sail, travelers may seek His bounty, and they may give thanks; easy movement leads to provision and remembrance.
Ships sail through the sea by God's favor, displaying signs to the steadfast and grateful; the moving vehicle is read as a blessing rather than a neutral tool.
Ships cleave the two seas so people may seek God's bounty and give thanks; travel, provision, and gratitude again share one vehicle-scene.
The flood subsides and the ark settles on Judi; this supplies the actual resting-place toward which the course and anchorage of 11:41 were directed.
Solomon has the horses returned and reaches toward their legs and necks; whatever the disputed action, the verse keeps attention on the ridden animal's very limbs and neck.
The required cow is explicitly untrained for plowing or watering fields; this gives a Qur'anic animal counterpart to the source-section's hard mount that has not yet been trained for work.
God creates creatures that move on bellies, two legs, and four; the four-footed gait places the section's careful transfer of the animal's limbs within a wider created order.
Once the prayer is finished, believers disperse through the land, seek God's bounty, and remember Him often; completed devotion opens into productive movement without losing zikr.
After the long daytime occupation of 73:7, the Prophet is told to remember his Lord's name and devote himself wholly to Him; exertion resolves into directed Godward attention.

The emigrant finds wide places and abundance in the earth, and one who leaves home toward God and His Messenger has an assured reward even if death overtakes him; the road is broad and its direction divine.
Twelve springs emerge and every people knows its drinking-place; the allocated water-stop parallels the she-camel's known turn without itself mentioning mounts.
Each of the twelve tribes knows its drinking-place and receives shade and food; ordered access to water is embedded in a fuller scene of travel provision.
The mountains are firmly set between the water-and-pasture verse and the declaration of provision; they form the fixed terrain through which the caravan moves.
Fruit and herbage are brought forth in the food passage; the herbage supplies the grazing side of the section's stopping-place.
The vegetation is provision for people and their livestock; road companions share what the land produces.
Water is driven to barren land and produces crops eaten by both livestock and people; divine provision restores the terrain needed by the travelling herd.
After Moses waters the animals, one woman returns with an invitation from her father to reward that service; the water-stop leads the traveler toward shelter and recompense.
“To your Lord is the return” restates the section's final direction, though without an accompanying travel scene.
